_comment: Curated 'mechanics' library for the crusades_1097 setting - see mechanics.py and engine.py's propose_mechanic_update tool, and settings/petrograd_1917/mechanics_catalog.json for the original pilot this follows. Each entry is a TYPE the AI may instantiate (never invent a type_key not listed here). seed_data is a historically-researched starting point.

crusader_princes_council.label: The Crusader Princes' Council — Relative Standing
crusader_princes_council.when_relevant: Create this once the council's own internal politics become something the player is actively navigating - plausible from campaign start, since the council already exists and Bohemond's standing within it is explicitly load-bearing for this whole setting (crusader_leaders_regard). IMPORTANT: this body has no formal seats or votes - factions.md is explicit that decisions happen through 'shifting coalitions, not a clean chain of command'. The seats below represent each prince's rough relative INFLUENCE/backing within the council (driven mainly by the size and quality of the forces they personally command), not a literal parliamentary body - make this framing clear if it ever surfaces in narration. Update it as a prince's standing shifts on-screen (a battlefield success, a public dispute, forces lost or reinforced). Expire only if the council itself dissolves as the expedition's leadership (not expected within this pack's near-term timeline).

data_shape.body_size: integer - total influence points, illustrative only, not a real seat count
data_shape.factions: array of {name, seats, note} - here 'seats' means relative influence/backing, not literal votes

crusader_princes_council.sourcing_note: Real leaders and rough relative force sizes per thecollector.com and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade: Raymond IV of Toulouse led the southern French contingent (commonly reckoned the single largest, alongside Adhemar's papal-sanctioned churchmen); Godfrey of Bouillon and his brother Baldwin of Boulogne led a large Lotharingian/German force; Bohemond of Taranto and his nephew Tancred led a smaller but famously disciplined, war-tested Italo-Norman contingent (veterans of real campaigns against the Byzantines themselves); Robert Curthose of Normandy, Robert II of Flanders, Stephen of Blois, and Hugh of Vermandois led smaller northern French/Flemish contingents. Adhemar of Le Puy, the papal legate, held influence well beyond his own modest personal force, as the expedition's spiritual authority. Chronicler troop totals for the whole expedition vary wildly (100,000 to 600,000 by different medieval chroniclers; modern historians estimate roughly 7,000 knights and 60,000 infantry total) - the relative proportions below are a reasoned illustrative split, not a precise census.

factions.name: Raymond of Toulouse & the Provençal host
factions.note: Commonly reckoned the single largest contingent - Raymond is also among the most senior and wealthiest of the princes.

factions.name: Godfrey of Bouillon & Baldwin (Lotharingia/Germany)
factions.note: A large, well-organized force from Lower Lorraine - Godfrey is broadly respected as level-headed among the princes.

factions.name: Bohemond of Taranto & Tancred (Italo-Norman)
factions.note: Smaller than Raymond's or Godfrey's numbers, but famously disciplined and war-tested - veterans of real campaigns against Byzantium itself. Bohemond's own ambitions (see byzantine_relations_ledger) make him the most independent-minded of the princes.

factions.name: Robert of Normandy & Robert of Flanders
factions.note: Solid northern French/Flemish contingents, generally aligned with each other.

factions.name: Stephen of Blois & Hugh of Vermandois
factions.note: Smaller prestige contingents - Hugh in particular trades on being the French king's brother more than on raw military weight.

factions.name: Adhemar of Le Puy (the papal legate)
factions.note: Modest personal force, but outsized influence as the expedition's spiritual authority and the pope's own representative - often the actual tie-breaker between rival princes.

byzantine_relations_ledger.label: The Oath to Alexios — Byzantine Relations Ledger
byzantine_relations_ledger.when_relevant: Create this at or near campaign start - the oath to Alexios is already a locked, sworn fact per canon_timeline.md (see the oath_to_alexios commitment), and it is the single most load-bearing piece of context for Bohemond's own arc specifically. This is a running ledger, not a chart - append a new entry each time the oath is tested, honored, or strained, rather than rewriting earlier entries. Update it as Byzantine relations shift on-screen. Expire only if the relationship is fully and finally severed (e.g. a clean, irreversible break with Byzantium) - a live possibility given this setting's central tension, but not something to assume.

data_shape.entries: array of {heading, tag, body} appended in chronological order - tag is a short date/status label, body is the actual ledger content. Prefer adding a new entry over rewriting old ones.

byzantine_relations_ledger.sourcing_note: Real terms and history per courses.lumenlearning.com and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Nicaea: in exchange for Byzantine food, supplies, and guides through Anatolia, Alexios I required the crusade's leaders to swear fealty and to promise that any territory recovered from the Turks that had formerly been Byzantine would be returned to the empire. Godfrey himself resisted swearing for months (citing prior loyalty to the Holy Roman Emperor) before finally taking the oath on 2 April 1097. The crusaders' first real test of the oath came almost immediately: Nicaea fell to them on 18 June 1097, and - notably, and to the rank and file's real resentment, since they'd expected to sack it themselves - the city was handed over to Byzantine forces rather than plundered, honoring the oath's letter even at real cost to morale.

entries.heading: The oath is sworn
entries.body: After months of resistance (Godfrey himself held out longest, citing prior loyalty to the Holy Roman Emperor), the crusade's leaders swear fealty to Alexios I and promise to return any recovered former Byzantine territory to the empire, in exchange for supplies, guides, and support through Anatolia.

entries.heading: Nicaea returned, not sacked
entries.body: Nicaea falls to the crusaders after a hard siege - but is handed over to Byzantine forces rather than plundered by the crusaders themselves, honoring the oath's letter. A real point of resentment among the rank and file, who had expected to sack it themselves.

crusader_host_at_antioch.label: The Crusader Host — Siege Deployment
crusader_host_at_antioch.when_relevant: Create this only once the canon 'Siege of Antioch begins' beat has actually fired - this campaign opens well before Antioch, and this mechanic has no reason to exist earlier. It represents the actual military deployment around the siege (who is blockading which gate, who commands the field army against relief attempts), which is a genuinely different picture from crusader_princes_council's standing/influence chart - both can coexist once the siege begins. Update it as the siege's specific deployments shift. Expire once the siege itself resolves (Antioch falls, and Kerbogha's relief army is in turn defeated) - the post-Antioch military picture (garrisoning the city, the march onward) would be a new mechanic instance if the campaign continues that far, not a continuation of this one.
crusader_host_at_antioch.sourcing_note: The long, grueling Siege of Antioch (beginning October 1097) is well documented as a multi-sided blockade effort by the assembled princes, each responsible for their own sector outside the city's walls, with Antioch's real fall (per canon_timeline.md) coming through betrayal/infiltration rather than a direct assault - and immediately followed by the crusaders themselves being besieged in turn by Kerbogha's relief force before defeating it. The seed below reflects the council's own real division of labor at a siege (each prince's contingent responsible for its own sector) rather than inventing a formal unified command that didn't really exist.

root.name: The Crusader Host, besieging Antioch
root.note: No single unified commander - each prince's contingent is responsible for its own sector of the blockade, coordinated (loosely) through the princes' council.

children.name: Raymond of Toulouse's sector
children.note: Provençal contingent, holding one approach to the city.

children.name: Bohemond and Tancred's sector
children.note: Italo-Norman contingent - Bohemond's eventual claim to the city (see byzantine_relations_ledger) has real roots in the leading role his forces play at this siege specifically.

children.name: Northern French/Flemish sector
children.note: Robert of Normandy, Robert of Flanders, and the smaller contingents, holding the remaining approaches.

antioch_siege_conditions.label: The Siege of Antioch — Conditions Ledger
antioch_siege_conditions.when_relevant: Create this once the canon 'Siege of Antioch begins' beat fires - alongside crusader_host_at_antioch (deployment) and crusader_princes_council (standing), this tracks a genuinely different axis: supply, morale, and desertion among the host as the siege actually grinds on. This is a running ledger, not a chart - append new entries as conditions change rather than rewriting old ones. Update it as morale/supply shift meaningfully on-screen. Expire once the siege resolves (Antioch falls and Kerbogha's relief army is defeated) - conditions inside a captured, garrisoned city would be a new mechanic if the campaign continues that far, not a continuation of this one.

data_shape.entries: array of {heading, tag, body} appended in chronological order - tag is a short date/status label, body is the actual ledger content. Prefer adding a new entry over rewriting old ones.

antioch_siege_conditions.sourcing_note: Real, well-documented and genuinely grim conditions, per worldhistory.org and historiesandcastles.com: the crusaders arrived outside Antioch on 21 October 1097 with too few men to fully encircle the city, which could still receive outside supplies. The winter of 1097-98 was brutal - supplies from Constantinople dwindled, foraging parties risked ambush, and by early 1098 roughly one in seven crusaders was dying of starvation, with horses, donkeys, camels, and even dogs eaten, and some reduced to boiling leather or digging up roots. The strain produced real desertion - most famously Stephen of Blois, one of the expedition's own named princes, who slipped away for Tarsus after seeing the scale of Kerbogha's relief army encamped nearby and concluding the crusade was doomed (a real, documented desertion by a named leader, not an invented complication).

entries.heading: The siege begins - too few men to fully encircle the city
entries.body: The host arrives outside Antioch's walls, but has too few men to close the blockade completely - Antioch can still receive supplies from outside, meaning this will be a long siege, not a quick one.

regional_muslim_powers.label: The Regional Political Landscape
regional_muslim_powers.when_relevant: Create this once the player is reasoning about the wider political landscape beyond Antioch's own walls specifically - the Seljuk world and Fatimid Egypt are explicitly, per this setting's own factions.md, 'not a monolith' and a plausible source of local alliance or negotiation, not just a united enemy. Most useful once the siege is underway and Kerbogha's relief force becomes a live threat, but can exist earlier if the player is already probing this landscape diplomatically. Update it as alliances shift or a new power becomes relevant on-screen. Expire only if this whole regional picture becomes moot to the campaign (not expected within this pack's near-term timeline).
regional_muslim_powers.sourcing_note: Named figures already have Monarch stat blocks in this setting's own npcs.md: Yaghi-Siyan, the capable Seljuk governor defending Antioch itself, and Kerbogha of Mosul, the powerful atabeg whose real relief army very nearly reverses the crusaders' victory just after Antioch falls. factions.md itself names Fatimid Egypt as a further, separate regional power with its own competing interests, distinct from the Seljuk Turks entirely (the two were rivals, not allies, in this period) - a real basis for the kind of local alliance or negotiation pure holy-war framing tends to obscure.

root.name: The Regional Powers Beyond Antioch
root.note: Not a monolith - real rivalries and competing interests run through this landscape as much as opposition to the crusade does.

children.name: Yaghi-Siyan, Governor of Antioch
children.note: A capable, experienced defender - not a pushover, right up until (and if) the historical betrayal that opens the city actually occurs.

children.name: Kerbogha of Mosul
children.note: A powerful Seljuk atabeg, not yet on the board - his real relief army arrives just as Antioch falls, nearly reversing the crusaders' victory.

children.name: The Wider Seljuk Sultanate
children.note: Genuinely fragmented, not a unified command - regional emirs and atabegs with their own, sometimes competing, priorities.

children.name: Fatimid Egypt
children.note: A separate, rival power to the Seljuk Turks entirely - a plausible, real basis for local negotiation or alliance that pure holy-war framing tends to obscure.
